title: Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp. (1999)
summary: The parties could not create a mandatory limited-fund class simply by agreeing how much the defendants would contribute.
notes:
The holding is bounded by the mandatory limited-fund theory presented. Do not merge the Rule 23(b)(1)(B) inquiry with Amchem’s Rule 23(b)(3) predominance analysis, although both decisions emphasize representation.

The vote was 7-2: Justice Souter wrote for the Court; Chief Justice Rehnquist concurred, joined by Scalia and Kennedy; Justice Breyer dissented, joined by Stevens, arguing the settlement made more money available to more claimants and the Court should have deferred to the district court. The certification was under Rule 23(b)(1)(B), and the Court required that the fund be limited by more than the parties' agreement and allocated through a process addressing conflicting interests.

sections.Parties: Asbestos claimants, Fibreboard, and its insurers proposed a global settlement through a Rule 23(b)(1)(B) class.
sections.Material Facts: The proposed fund arose from negotiations while insurance coverage was disputed. The arrangement excluded substantial groups of existing claimants, included present and future claimants with different interests, and grouped together people whose claims implicated different insurance coverage. Fibreboard would retain virtually all of its net worth. Class members could not simply opt out and pursue the ordinary route available in a damages class.
sections.Procedural History: The district court certified the mandatory class and approved the settlement; the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court reversed.
sections.Issue: Did the negotiated arrangement establish a limited fund and equitable treatment sufficient to justify binding the class without opt-out rights?
sections.Holding: No. The record did not establish the relevant fund limitations and protections required for the proposed mandatory class.
sections.Reasoning: The Court required an evidentiary basis for the fund’s upper limit and insufficiency rather than accepting the negotiating parties’ numbers. It also examined whether the class included the relevant competing claimants and whether distributions treated their interests equitably. Present and future claims, and claims with different access to insurance, created conflicts requiring structurally independent representation. The absence of opt-out rights increased the significance of these protections. The Court identified the company’s retention of its assets as a further serious difficulty, while reserving whether that feature alone would invalidate the settlement and whether some credit for litigation-cost savings could ever be appropriate.

learning.why: The parties could not create a mandatory limited-fund class simply by agreeing how much the defendants would contribute.

topics.cp-limited-fund: The limit and insufficiency of the fund needed independent evidentiary support.
topics.cp-adequate-representation: Materially different present, future, and insurance-coverage interests required separate protection.
topics.cp-settlement-class: Agreement on a settlement amount did not establish the prerequisites for a mandatory class.
topics.cp-frcp-23: The decision construes Rule 23(b)(1)(B) and its historical limited-fund antecedents.
topics.cp-class-certification: Ortiz sets the showing required to certify a mandatory limited-fund class.
topics.cp-rules-enabling: The Court read Rule 23(b)(1)(B) narrowly partly to avoid Rules Enabling Act and Seventh Amendment concerns with mandatory classes.

mnemonic.rationale: A limited fund that was not limited
